Issued at 455 AM CDT Thu Sep 24 2026

A shortwave trough axis is located over central North Dakota 
early this morning, moving northeast. Showers and thunderstorms 
associated with the shortwave have mostly exited our forecast 
area, with the exception of the southern James River Valley. 
Chances for showers and storms there greatly diminish after 
sunrise. Weak surface flow under cyclonic flow aloft has allowed
widespread low clouds and dense fog to develop. The lowest 
visibility is located throughout western and into north central 
North Dakota, where a Dense Fog Advisory remains in effect until
11 AM CDT. The fog and stratus should clear from west to east 
later this morning through the afternoon, giving way to 
plentiful sunshine. A mid to upper level ridge building behind 
the departing shortwave will also bring warmer temperatures back
into the region today, with afternoon highs in the lower 70s 
east to lower 80s far west. Deep layer subsidence with weak 
winds could yield another round of dense fog late tonight into 
Friday morning, this time more focused from south central to 
northeast North Dakota. Lows tonight are forecast in the mid 
40s to mid 50s.

Mid to upper level high pressure will slide towards the Great 
Lakes on Friday as a potent trough lands on the Pacific 
Northwest. In between these 2 features, a shortwave with a WNW-
ESE oriented axis is forecast to eject north/northeastward off 
the Central Rockies, reaching the Northern Plains Friday 
evening. Forecast timing of the shortwave has slowed to the 
point we are now confident in mostly dry weather during the day 
Friday, although low clouds could expand from southeast to 
northwest during the afternoon. Forecast highs on Friday are in 
the upper 60s to mid 70s, but aside from the far west, this 
seems a little too warm given the expected moisture-rich 
southeast surface flow and potential cloud cover. Another 
change from previous forecasts is that both chances for rain 
and QPF Friday evening into Saturday morning have decreased. 
Current PoPs are still around 20 percent in central North 
Dakota to as high as 65 percent in the southern James River 
Valley, but the probability of QPF exceeding just one tenth of 
an inch is very low outside of the James River Valley. 

Dry weather is anticipated Saturday into Sunday as the Pacific 
Northwest trough lifts into northern Alberta/Saskatchewan, 
forming a stacked and occluded cyclone. A cold/occluded front 
is still projected to enter western North Dakota during the day 
Saturday, but the strength of winds both ahead of and behind the
front has lowered from previous forecasts. Highs this weekend 
are mostly projected in the upper 60s to mid 70s, but slightly 
cooler in the northwest on Sunday due to the influence of a 
southern Canadian high pressure. The cold/occluded front is 
projected to stall roughly from the northern Red River Valley 
to the Black Hills Sunday morning and transition to a northward 
lifting warm front Sunday afternoon as another deep trough lands
on the Pacific coast. Low chances for rain enter western North 
Dakota as early as Sunday afternoon, but greatly increase and 
expand statewide Sunday evening into Monday as a shortwave 
ejects from the base of the deeper trough. The lead shortwave 
looks to depart to the northeast Monday morning, but strong 
synoptic scale lift from DCVA with a northern stream wave and 
dynamics from a coupled jet keeps high chances for rain in the 
forecast through Monday. Ensemble spread has greatly diminished 
in the last 24 hours, with all clusters now painting medium to 
high chances for exceeding half an inch of rain from Sunday 
evening through Monday afternoon, broadly focused over North 
Dakota. An axis of highest QPF threshold probabilities over 
this time frame can be visualized from southwest to northeast 
North Dakota, although there are subtle shifts among each 
cluster. Lending further confidence to a rainier outcome is the
presence of 90th-99th climatological percentile precipitable 
water in both NAEFS and ECMWF guidance. There is also a risk 
for thunderstorms through Monday afternoon, with ensemble mean 
MUCAPE projected as high as 1000 J/kg. This may be accompanied 
by a conditional risk for severe thunderstorms in what could be 
a strongly sheared environment, and a signal for this has been 
showing up in CSU machine learning guidance.

Uncertainty in the progression of the northern stream does 
reemerge on Tuesday, which could determine how quickly rain 
ends from west to east. By the middle of the week, ensemble 
spread in the synoptic pattern increases to the point that it 
is difficult to determine any potential outcome being favored 
over others. The NBM does show a distinct cooling trend through
Tuesday, when forecast highs are limited to the upper 50s and 
lower 60s. At this time, NBM 25th percentile low temperatures
